summary: Describes the operational convention of placing certain DNS records under a reserved node name that begins with an underscore, such as _name, beneath the domain they apply to. It sets up an IANA registry for these names so uses do not collide. It is a Best Current Practice.

plainLanguage.summary: Some DNS services need to attach their own records to a domain without inventing a new record type. This document describes the convention they use: put the records under a branch whose first label starts with an underscore, and register that label so no two services use the same one.

subtitle: How DNS names that start with an underscore scope a record to its parent domain, and the IANA registry that keeps them from colliding.

tldr.problem: The DNS assigns no meaning to names, so two services that both want to store a TXT record under the same domain cannot tell their records apart.
tldr.mechanism: A service places its records under a branch whose first name starts with an underscore, such as _domainkey, and that name is registered with IANA so that no two services claim the same one.
tldr.outcome: A client asking for one service's data gets only that service's records, and different services cannot collide over a name. RFC 8552 is an Internet Best Current Practice.

today: RFC 8552 is an Internet Best Current Practice, published in March 2019. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so the guidance stands as written.

sections.title: Why Underscored Names Exist
sections.content:
The core DNS specifications assign no semantics to domain names or their parts, and set no constraints on which resource record types may be stored under which names. Over time some leaf names, such as www and ftp, have come to imply support for particular services, but that is operational convention rather than defined protocol semantics. This freedom has allowed a wide range of administrative and semantic policies to run side by side.

DNS data semantics have been limited to the specification of particular resource record types, on the expectation that new types would be added as needed. Adding a new type has proved extremely challenging, with significant adoption and use barriers over the life of the DNS.

The underscored naming convention is the alternative: instead of a new record type, a service uses an existing record type but places it in a restricted scope. The scoped data sits under a leaf node whose parent is the domain the data actually applies to. The branch under that parent is indicated by a sequence of one or more reserved node names, and at least the first, that is the highest, of those names begins with an underscore.

The DNS rules for a host name do not allow the underscore character, so an underscored name is distinguishable from every legal host name. The convention therefore creates a space for listing attributes, in the form of resource record types, that belong to the parent domain above the underscored branch.

The convention is particularly useful with generalised record types such as TXT, SRV and URI. It separates one use of them from others. Without that separation, an undifferentiated mass of records is returned to the client, which then has to parse through all of them hoping to find the relevant ones, and in some cases the results are ambiguous because a record type does not adequately identify its own purpose. With underscore-based scoping, only the relevant record sets come back.
sections.plainLanguage: The DNS deliberately says nothing about what names mean, so services cannot tell each other apart by name alone. Instead, a service hangs its records under a label that starts with an underscore, a character no host name can contain, and that makes the records easy to separate and to look up.

sections.title: How Underscore-Based Scoping Works
sections.content:
Scope here means a static property of the DNS name, not something that depends on the nature of the query. The scope is a leaf node holding the resource record sets that are formally defined and constrained.

The example given is DomainKeys Identified Mail, which uses _domainkey to define a place to hold a TXT record containing signing information for the parent domain. The name _domainkey.example. acts as an attribute of the parent domain name example..

The convention is also about scale. Some record types are used in a way that creates scaling problems when the whole record set for a domain is gathered at the leaf node for that name. Instead of putting the records at the node that would otherwise hold them, an increasingly popular approach places them under a specially named branch beneath that node. The rules for naming that branch define the context for interpreting the record set. A direct lookup at the subordinate leaf node then produces only the desired record types, at no greater cost than a typical DNS lookup.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of putting a service's records at example.com, they go at _domainkey.example.com. A client that asks for that name gets the service's records and nothing else, and it costs one ordinary lookup.

sections.title: Global Underscored Node Names
sections.content:
The DNS uses names organised in a tree. A domain name might have several node names beginning with an underscore. The global underscored node name is the one closest to the root of the DNS hierarchy, the highest or topmost. In the presentation convention of Section 3.1 of RFC 1034 this is the rightmost name that begins with an underscore; in other presentation environments it may sit elsewhere, which is why the word global is used.

To avoid collisions between services using the same underscored name with the same record type, the document establishes the Underscored and Globally Scoped DNS Node Names registry with IANA. Use of node names beginning with an underscore is reserved when the underscored name is the one closest to the DNS root, in which case it is considered global. Underscored names farther down the hierarchy are handled within the scope of the global underscored node name.
sections.plainLanguage: A name may have several underscore labels in it. The registry only records the topmost one, because that is the part that has to be unique across the whole Internet. The lower parts are the business of whoever registered the top one.

sections.title: Wildcards and Underscored Names
sections.content:
DNS wildcards interact badly with underscored names in two ways. Since wildcards are only interpreted as leaf names, one cannot create the equivalent of a wildcard name for prefixed names: a name such as label.*.example.com is not a wildcard. Conversely, a wildcard such as *.example.com can match any name, including an underscored name, so a wildcard might match an underscored name and return a record of the type that the underscored name controls but that is not intended for the underscored context and does not conform to its rules.

The document also records the history. Different uses of underscored node names developed largely without coordination. For TXT records there is no consistent internal syntax that lets one tell the different uses apart. For the SRV and URI records, telling the different uses apart was part of the design, and those specifications serve as templates defining records that might only be used for specific applications when there is an additional specification. The SRV template referred to two levels of tables of names, a local scope set of _service names and a global scope field of _proto. The aggregate effect of these independent efforts was a long list of underscored names reserved without coordination, which invites an eventual name-assignment collision. The remedy is this document and a companion one, RFC 8553, which define a registry for the names and try to register those already in use.
sections.plainLanguage: Wildcards and underscored names do not mix well. A wildcard matches any name, so it can hand back a record that belongs to the underscored branch without following the rules of that branch. The document also explains how the collection of underscored names grew up without coordination, which is why a registry is needed.

sections.title: The Registry and Its Rules
sections.content:
If a public specification calls for the use of an underscored node name, the global underscored node name, the one closest to the DNS root, MUST be entered into the registry.

An underscored name defines the scope of use for specific record types, which are associated with the domain name that is the parent of the branch the underscored name defines. A given name defines a specific, constrained context for one or more record types, and use of those types inside it conforms to the defined constraints. Within a leaf that is underscore scoped, other record sets that are not part of the scope MAY be used.

Structurally the registry is a single, flat table of record types under node names beginning with an underscore. In some cases the full scoping name is multi-part, a sequence of underscored names, and semantically that sequence represents a hierarchical model. It is reasonable to reuse a subordinate underscored name in a different global context, because a subordinate name is meaningful only within the scope of the global underscored node name, so subordinate names are ignored by this registry. The registry is for the definition of the highest-level, global, underscored node name.

The use of underscored node names is specific to each record type being scoped. Each name defines a place, but does not define the rules for what appears underneath that place, either as further underscored naming or as a leaf node with resource records. Those rules come from the specifications for individual record types. Definition and registration of subordinate underscored node names are the responsibility of the specification that creates the global registry entry, so each registered global underscored node name owns a distinct subordinate namespace.

The registry includes any DNS node name that begins with the underscore character, ASCII 0x5F, and is the underscored node name closest to the root. It operates under the IANA rules for Expert Review. Every entry MUST contain values for all the fields, and the combination of record type and node name MUST be unique. The table is maintained sorted by record type and then by node name. The required reference for an entry must have a stable resolution to the organisation controlling that entry.

An entry holds three fields. The record type lists a type defined for use within the scope. The node name specifies a single underscored name that defines a reserved name, the global entry name for the scoped record types associated with it, and characters that have an upper and a lower case form MUST be recorded in lower case to simplify name comparisons. The reference lists the specification that defines the record type and its use under the node name, and the organisation producing that specification retains control of the registry entry.

Each record type used with a node name MUST have a separate registry entry. The document also gives specification writers a template for requesting a new entry, with the record type, the node name and the citation.
sections.plainLanguage: The registry has one row for each pair of record type and underscored name, and the pair must be unique. The record is lower case. The reference field points at the document that defines the use, and whoever wrote that document keeps control of the entry.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
IANA has established the Underscored and Globally Scoped DNS Node Names registry. The section describes the registry, the definitions, the initial entries, the use of _ta and _example, and the use of RFC 8126 as guidance for expert review. IANA has also updated the Enumservices Registrations registry with a pointer to this document.

Two special entries are explained. Under the NULL record type, the entry _ta-* denotes all node names beginning with the string _ta-*; it does not refer to a DNS wildcard specification. The node name _example is reserved across all record sets.

The initial contents include _example for all record types, _ta-* for NULL, _openpgpkey for OPENPGPKEY, _smimecert for SMIMEA, and a set of SRV names such as _dccp, _http, _ipv6, _ldap, _ocsp, _sctp, _sip, _tcp, _udp and _xmpp. For TLSA there are _dane, _sctp and _udp. For TXT there are _acme-challenge, _dmarc, _domainkey, _mta-sts, _spf, _sztp, _tcp, _udp and _vouch. For URI there is a long list of names covering the many telephone and messaging services, such as _acct, _email, _fax, _h323, _sip, _sms, _web and _xmpp.
sections.plainLanguage: The registry starts with the names already in use, so that existing services keep working and new ones can check whether a name is taken.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: This memo raises no security issues. It defines a naming convention and a registry for it, and does not change how records under those names are published.
sections.plainLanguage: The document raises no security questions of its own.
